_about: Every visitor-facing string of the EU rules tool (Rulebook in Motion), checked by the style gate. The tool stands on its own: the only Atlas pages it names are country profiles, linked by their full address and only when the page passes them. The outcome labels are fixed by the brief. The question, lede, standing note, scope line, method note and link labels are drafts until Swann has reviewed them. The legal time limits after an incident are called reporting deadlines throughout (spec 13). The strings from question to nextEuProfile are rendered by the server only and never reach the island; standing is the note on compliance, written once, under the question.

copy.question: Which EU cyber rules plausibly apply to an organisation?
copy.lede: A few answers about an organisation, matched against {acts} EU acts and the reporting deadlines they set.
copy.description: Which of {acts} EU cyber acts plausibly apply to an organisation, from its sector, size and answers, with the reporting deadlines one incident can start. EU instruments only.
copy.scopeMany: These rules govern cybersecurity in general; {crypto} of their {obligations} obligations mention cryptography.
copy.scopeOne: These rules govern cybersecurity in general; {crypto} of their {obligations} obligations mentions cryptography.
copy.scopeNone: These rules govern cybersecurity in general; none of their {obligations} obligations mentions cryptography.
copy.scopeNoCount: These rules govern cybersecurity in general.
copy.standing: EU instruments only, and not legal advice: this tool does not tell you whether you are compliant. Confirm obligations with counsel.
copy.method: The tool reads {acts} EU instruments and, within them, only the articles that decide who is in scope and what happens after an incident. It does not read national law, guidance or supervisory practice, and Member States can extend the scope of these rules and add requirements when they transpose them. Your answers are matched against rules written as data, each citing the paragraph it comes from; the most specific matching rule sets the outcome, and every rule that matched is listed with its article. An answer of “not sure” is never read as “no”: it can only make an outcome more cautious. The reporting deadlines differ in what they are counted from: some from becoming aware of an incident, one from classifying it as major, one from a fix becoming available, so the rows do not share a starting line. An obligation counts as mentioning cryptography when the law’s own words for it, the paragraph it comes from and the excerpt quoted, name cryptography or encryption; the plain-language summaries are not read for this. Commission proposals appear only when you ask for them, drawn dashed and labelled as proposals with their current stage. The acts and procedures are checked against EUR-Lex metadata every week.
